Gödel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursively Self-Improvement

Xunjian Yin, Xinyi Wang, Liangming Pan, Li Lin, Xiaojun Wan, William Yang Wang

Paper ↗arXiv ↗Code ↗Blog ↗

Gödel Agent can inspect and rewrite its own running code, using task feedback to revise both its problem-solving policy and the procedure that improves it.

01 / The research question

What if the procedure that improves an agent could improve too?

A prompt optimizer can revise the solver while keeping its own search routine fixed. That routine still decides which changes to propose, how to test them, what feedback to retain, and how to recover from an error. Gödel Agent makes this outer procedure editable as well: the agent can inspect and rewrite the code that solves tasks and the code that organizes subsequent revisions.

The practical consequence is a larger choice of computations. An agent can change a prompt, add a verifier, replace an LLM call with an algorithm, or improve the diagnostics used to make the next edit. The Game of 24 cases show these choices in actual code. The central question is whether access to its own implementation helps an agent find better policies from task feedback.

02 / Explore the idea
Case study · Game of 24

From asking for an expression to searching for one

Use four numbers exactly once, with +, −, ×, ÷ and parentheses, to make 24. In one reported run, six unsuccessful optimization attempts led the agent to replace its LLM-based solver with a search algorithm.

Initial policy

Listing 5 ↗
def solver(numbers):
    prompt = describe_game(numbers)
    response = call_language_model(prompt)
    return response

The model proposes the expression. Whether it obeys the rules depends on its generated answer.

Rewritten policy

Listing 6 ↗
def search(values):
    if one_value_remains(values):
        return equals_24(values[0])
    for a, b, operation in choices(values):
        reduced = apply(a, b, operation)
        if search(reduced):
            return solution

Code checks combinations of numbers and operations. A solved expression no longer needs an LLM call.

Condensed pseudocode of the published policies. The structural change is from generated answers to explicit search; the appendix contains the full Python implementations.

A different run · original paper figure

Other runs kept the LLM—and changed the surrounding code

The paper also documents an LLM-based path: add code-assisted verification, recover from a formatting error, try additional candidates, and revise the checks. The original curve shows that changes can help, fail, or be reverted. This is a different trajectory from the switch to search above.

03 / Inside the method

Revisions change the running program

The implementation exposes Python variables, functions and classes through runtime inspection. A language model reads this state, selects actions, and can install replacement code through monkey patching. Its four core actions are to inspect the current implementation, interact with the task environment, update code, and continue improvement. Recursive invocation lets later iterations enter the revised improvement function.

This gives feedback two distinct roles. Validation examples assess the task policy. Execution errors diagnose the implementation of an edit. When an action fails, the supplied error-handling mechanism stops that action sequence and carries the error into the next step. The next revision can therefore change the solver, the way errors are interpreted, or the procedure that selects and applies changes.

The objective and the initial tools still come from the designer. Self-reference makes more of the program available for revision; it does not eliminate the need for a useful evaluation signal, nor does it supply a proof that a proposed edit will improve performance. The empirical implementation uses LLM-generated modifications rather than the formal proof search of a theoretical Gödel machine.

  1. 01

    Inspect its implementation

    Expose the agent's functions, variables, and current policy through runtime introspection.

  2. 02

    Modify running code

    An LLM proposes changes and applies them through Python monkey patching.

  3. 03

    Evaluate and iterate

    Task feedback and error traces inform subsequent changes to the policy and improvement process.

04 / Reading the evidence

A strong gain in multilingual math, with smaller gains elsewhere

  • 64.2%

    MGSM · Gödel-base

    Under the closed-book GPT-3.5 setup, test accuracy exceeds Meta Agent Search's 53.4% on multilingual mathematical reasoning.

  • 80.9 F1

    DROP · Gödel-base

    The constrained agent improves over the reported 79.4 F1 for Meta Agent Search on reading comprehension requiring discrete reasoning.

Under the constrained Gödel-base setting, the optimized policies use GPT-3.5 at task execution time. MGSM accuracy increases from Meta Agent Search’s 53.4% to 64.2%. Improvements are smaller on reading comprehension, general knowledge and graduate-level science. The full table below preserves the uncertainty and makes those differences visible.

The agent that proposes code changes uses GPT-4o. This is distinct from the model used by the resulting task policy. Gödel-free relaxes the execution constraints too, and can call stronger models while solving the task. Keeping these settings separate is necessary to understand which part of the performance gain comes from agent design and which comparison also permits stronger tools.

All four tasks, with uncertainty visible

The largest gap over Meta Agent Search is on MGSM: +10.8 percentage points. DROP, MMLU and GPQA show smaller point-estimate gains, with overlapping confidence intervals for these three tasks. The table does not establish a decisive advantage on every task.

What about the higher Gödel-free scores?

DROP F1 90.5 ± 1.8, MGSM accuracy 90.6 ± 2.0, MMLU accuracy 87.9 ± 2.2, GPQA accuracy 55.7 ± 3.1. This version may call stronger models, including GPT-4o, while solving tasks. Its scores measure unrestricted tool use and belong to a different comparison from Gödel-base.

What makes continued improvement possible?

Removing error handling reduces MGSM accuracy from 64.2% to 49.4%. An agent that rewrites code needs a way to observe and recover from bad edits.

    64.2%
  • Without thinking before acting
    50.8%
  • Without error handling
    49.4%
  • Without code-running tool
    57.1%
  • Without LLM-calling tool
    60.4%

Self-improvement is not monotonic

Across 100 MGSM optimization trials:

92%
encountered a temporary performance drop
14%
finished below the initial policy
4%
terminated unexpectedly

These are different, potentially overlapping events—not three parts of a whole. Editing the improvement procedure can also break the ability to continue improving.

Research summary

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents across various tasks. However, existing agentic systems, whether based on fixed pipeline algorithms or pre-defined meta-learning frameworks, cannot search the whole agent design space due to the restriction of human-designed components, and thus might miss the more optimal agent design. In this paper, we introduce Gödel Agent, a self-evolving framework inspired by the Gödel Machine, enabling agents to recursively improve themselves without relying on predefined routines or fixed optimization algorithms. Gödel Agent leverages LLMs to dynamically modify its own logic and behavior, guided solely by high-level objectives through prompting. Experimental results on multiple domains demonstrate that the implementation of Gödel Agent can achieve continuous self-improvement, surpassing manually crafted agents in performance, efficiency, and generalizability.
